1.pericope_label: The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius; that thou mayest prosper and be in health

schools.summary: The identification of the recipient is the first thing the hearers will ask about, so give the evidence and say honestly how far it goes. The difference in date alone is enough to separate this man from the Caius who was Paul's host at Corinth, and nothing in the letter shows whether he was a presbyter. Then correct the prayer, because the English misleads: the phrase rendered "above all things" means in respect of all things, not more than anything else, and on the common rendering the apostle would be wishing his friend bodily health above his salvation, which cannot be meant. The words are worth a moment each -- the verb for prospering is built on the roots for a good journey, and the verb for health, which elsewhere in the New Testament means soundness of doctrine, here means the body. Note that the comparison assumes the welfare of the man's soul before measuring anything against it.

Settle the identification by chronology rather than by sentiment: Paul's Caius lived at Corinth and this one somewhere near Ephesus, the one was contemporary with Paul and the other with John, and there are thirty or forty years between them; the Corinthian was baptized by Paul and was his spiritual child, whereas this man is John's. Then keep the first clause of the prayer on the ground where it belongs. To prosper here means success in temporal affairs, in the business of life; and since success of that kind depends on the blessing which maketh rich, it is a proper thing to ask of God and not a worldly intrusion into a spiritual letter.

Take the recipient to be the Corinthian whom Paul names, and say what follows if he is: either he had removed from Achaia into Asia, or this letter was sent to Corinth. Then divide the prayer into its three petitions and preach them as three -- health of body, health of soul, and prosperity in secular affairs -- adding that every Christian may in some measure expect all three, that every Christian is authorised to pray for them, and that we should have more of all three if we prayed for them devoutly. It is worth mentioning that a manuscript turns the second clause into a wish that the man be sound in the truth. On the writer's self-description, note only that the reticence of the title is itself part of the letter's tenderness.

Begin with the writer's refusal of a grander title. He might have assumed many more illustrious characters, but it does not become Christ's ministers to affect swelling pompous titles; he almost levels himself with the ordinary pastors, or else, the extraordinary ministers being now dead, he takes the common name in order to countenance the standing ministry that remains. Then give the congregation the aphorism the passage yields. There is such a thing as soul-prosperity, and it is the greatest blessing on this side heaven. Grace and health are two rich companions: grace will improve health and health will employ grace. Admit the hard case, that a rich soul is often lodged in a crazy body and grace must then submit to the dispensation. And close where it stings, that for most professors the apostle's wish would have to be reversed before it could honestly be prayed.

sides.position: Not Paul's Corinthian host: that man lived at Corinth and this one near Ephesus, the one was contemporary with Paul and the other with John, thirty or forty years apart, and the Corinthian was Paul's convert while this is John's
The difference in date alone is sufficient reason against any attempt at identification with the men named in Acts and Romans; nor is there anything to show whether he was a presbyter
Probably the Caius of Corinth whom Paul mentions; if so, either he had removed from Achaia into Asia, or the letter was sent to Corinth
Five men of the name occur; this one is thought by some critics to be different from all, since the apostle ranks him among his children
If this is not Paul's host, it is his brother in name, estate and disposition
Nothing more is known of him

debates.question: What does "above all things" mean in the prayer?

sides.position: In respect of all things, not more than anything else; on the common rendering the apostle would be wishing health and outward prosperity above his friend's usefulness or salvation, which cannot be the meaning
The prayer has three parts, health of body, health of soul and prosperity in secular affairs, and every Christian is authorised to pray for all three
Success in temporal affairs and the business of life, which depends on the blessing that maketh rich and is therefore to be prayed for
A remarkable comparison, which assumes the welfare of his soul and measures the rest against it

outliers.note: Alone enumerates the five men of this name in the New Testament and distinguishes them one from another -- Paul's host at Corinth, the Caius baptized there, the Macedonian who travelled with Paul, the Caius of Derbe known by his epithet, and this one -- arguing that the host of the Corinthian church would hardly have left the city to travel in Asia.

Alone reads the writer's bare self-description as a deliberate refusal of rank, observing that he might have assumed many more illustrious characters but that it does not become Christ's ministers to affect swelling pompous titles, and suggesting that the extraordinary ministers being now dead he took the commoner name to countenance the standing ministry that remained.

Alone corrects the received rendering of the prayer, showing that the phrase means in respect of all things rather than more than anything else, and alone remarks that the wish is the reverse of the one we are commonly constrained to express for our friends, whose spiritual interests usually lag so far behind the rest that it is benevolence to wish them as prosperous in religion as in everything else.

themes: The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth
Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth

3.pericope_label: No greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth

schools.summary: Two small points of grammar carry more than they look. The verb of rejoicing is not the epistolary aorist but a report of what the writer felt when the news reached him, and the participles mark repetition -- brethren arriving from time to time and testifying each time they came. The word for greater is a double comparative built on a comparative, the formation that gives us "lesser," and the like of it turns up in the papyri, in Homer and in Shakespeare. Note also that the pronoun is emphatic, this man being set deliberately against the one named later in the letter, and that in these writings truth covers the moral, intellectual and spiritual spheres together. On "my children," say that the word may imply the writer's own converts, and leave it there.

Take the passage as an account of how a good report is made and who owes it. The thing testified was the truth in the man, that is the reality of his faith, evinced by his charity; faith should work by love, and gains its lustre by the offices of love. The witnesses were the brethren who had received good from him, and a good report is due from those who have received good -- though a good name is a small enough reward for costly service, it is better than precious ointment and will not be refused by the ingenuous. The hearing was before the church, and it is worth guessing why: either out of the fulness of the heart the mouth spoke, or they wished to engage the congregation's prayers that such a patron might be continued to them.

Identify the travellers plainly as preachers of the word who went from place to place to spread the gospel, since everything later in the letter depends on their being that. Then handle the variant at the fourth verse rather than passing it: the Latin reads grace or thanks where the received text reads joy, which would make the sense that the apostle had nothing to be more thankful for. Keep the exposition close to the words and do not build a doctrine on the affectionate address; what the verse asserts is that the reality of a man's religion shows itself in his walk, and that this was what the report established.

The disputed word here is "children," and the temptation is to make it settle the question of who converted this man. Resist that. The inference has been drawn that he must have been John's convert and therefore not the Corinthian, but an aged man has a right to address his juniors in age and grace by that name, and there is propriety and dignity in it coming from such a person; the term is the tender style of paternal love, whoever the instrument of conversion was, and it has a peculiar beauty from a writer who calls himself the elder. Then say what the verse is really about, that such is the spirit of every true Christian pastor -- and widen it, since the same is the highest joy of every Christian parent, at home or with children abroad.

debates.question: Does calling him a child mean the writer converted him?

sides.position: Yes: this is the language of an aged apostle about converts who looked up to him as a father, so Gaius was probably converted under his ministry and was much the younger man
By the use of the word John may mean that Gaius is one of his converts
It has been inferred so, and thence that he is not the Corinthian; but an old man had a right to address his juniors in age and grace by that name, and there is propriety and dignity in it
Caius was probably converted by Paul, so the word is the tender style of paternal love whoever the instrument was, and has a peculiar beauty from a writer calling himself the elder

outliers.note: Alone notes that the word for greater is a double comparative built on a comparative, the formation that yields "lesser" in English, with parallels in the vernacular papyri, in Homer and in Shakespeare; and alone records the manuscript that reads grace where the text has joy -- a variant Gill reaches independently from the Latin side.

Alone attends to the making of the report rather than its content, holding that a good report is owed by those who have received good, that a good name though a small reward for costly service is better than precious ointment, and guessing that the travellers testified before the church in order to engage its prayers for the continued life and usefulness of such a patron.

Alone extends the apostle's joy from ministers to parents, holding that a child who wished to confer the greatest possible happiness on his family could do it in no other way, and that nothing gives a Christian more peace in dying than assurance on that point.

themes: For I rejoiced greatly, when the brethren came and testified of the truth that is in thee, even as thou walkest in the truth
I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth

5.pericope_label: Thou doest faithfully to the brethren and to strangers; fellowhelpers to the truth

schools.summary: Say where the text is uncertain and where it is not. The opening phrase may mean a faithful work or "thou makest sure," and the point cannot be settled. Sending forward, by contrast, is a definite thing: a custom running back to Homer of speeding the parting guest, sometimes by accompanying him and sometimes by providing money and food, and the rabbis were escorted so. The formula translated "thou wilt do well" is the ordinary polite request of the letters preserved on papyrus. Take the bare use of "the Name" as the sum of the Christian creed, like the absolute use of "the Way" in Acts. And draw the conclusion the passage licenses about the other letter: so warm a praise of hospitality here shows that the refusal of hospitality urged in the second epistle was aimed at a particular case, not laid down as a rule.

Keep the motive in view before the act. What is commended is faithfulness, and the point of the word is that the giving was not done in a hypocritical way, to be seen of men and gain their applause, but from a principle of love and with a view to the glory of God. Then make the occasion concrete: these brethren went out from Judea, either of their own accord to preach the gospel or driven out by the unbelieving Jews for professing the name, and either way there was reason they should be regarded. Note that the testimony was borne before the whole congregation and that the apostle mentions it in order to encourage a continuance of the same kindness to the same men, who are now on their way back.

This is the passage to preach on the support of ministers, and the sources give you leave to be blunt. Ask whether congregations who owe their preachers nothing by law deal with them in a manner worthy of God, or leave them lacking the bread that perishes while they minister the bread of life without sparing; note that in the apostolic mission each church bore the cost of sending a man on to the next. Balance it, though, with the maxim that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and observe that the congregations which bear the whole expense of the gospel are the ones that prize it most. One alternative reading is worth mentioning: that the participle governs what follows, so that these men were driven out by the Gentiles and went with nothing, having left their property behind.

debates.question: What does the phrase rendered "thou doest faithfully" mean?

sides.position: Either a faithful work or "thou makest sure," on a parallel from Xenophon; it is not certain
The adjective may stand for the noun, so that it means keeping the faith or one's engagements; the sense is that he acted as the Christian religion required
A faithful thing, done not hypocritically to be seen of men and gain applause, but from a principle of love and to the glory of God
Uprightly and sincerely

debates.question: Why did the missionaries take nothing of the Gentiles?

sides.position: From prudential considerations, lest it hinder their success and expose them to the charge of a mercenary spirit
So that Christian missionaries should receive nothing from the heathen; there were many travelling lecturers out for money, and the charge has had to be guarded against since

On some occasions this may be necessary, but the maxim of the founder of the religion is that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and the congregations that bear the whole expense prize the gospel most. Alternatively the participle governs what follows: they were driven out by the Gentiles and went taking nothing, leaving their property behind
They went forth from Judea, either of their own accord to preach or driven out by the unbelieving Jews for professing the name

outliers.note: Alone draws an inference from this passage back to the second epistle, arguing that so warm a praise of hospitality here shows the refusal of hospitality urged there to have been aimed at a peculiar case rather than laid down as a rule; and alone traces the custom of speeding a parting guest back to Homer, noting that rabbis were escorted so and that the polite formula for "thou wilt do well" is the ordinary please of the letter-writing papyri.

Alone turns the verse on the reader's own congregation, asking whether churches whose preachers can claim nothing by law deal with them in a manner worthy of God or leave them lacking the bread that perishes while they minister the bread of life without sparing; and alone proposes that the participle governs the following phrase, so that the missionaries were driven out by the Gentiles and went with nothing, leaving their property behind in destitution.

themes: Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers
Because that for his name's sake they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles
We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth

9.pericope_label: Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence, receiveth us not

schools.summary: Handle the textual question first and do not let it slide: a few copies add a particle that would turn "I wrote" into "I would have written," and the addition is not sustained by good authority. The letter referred to is therefore a real one, now lost, most likely a brief note of commendation, and not the second epistle. On the man himself, the verb describing his ambition is so rare as to be found here and afterwards only in church writers; be careful what you build on it, since loving the first place does not prove him a bishop set over elders, an arrangement belonging to the next century -- he may have been an elder or a deacon and still have wanted to rule the whole church. The verbs for hindering and casting out may each describe one success, a settled practice, or an attempt that failed.

Adopt the conditional rendering and explain what it buys you: the apostle would have written to the church, but knew his letter must pass through the hands of a man who would not acknowledge his authority, and so wrote to a private member instead. That makes sense of the whole letter. On the man's conduct, give the congregation a phrase they will remember -- he had the entire principle of the dog in the manger, neither doing nor letting do, and undoing whatever good was done that he did not approve. Guess at the motive if you like, that he may have been a converted Jew unwilling to see Gentiles admitted, or a Judaizer who slandered the apostles for teaching otherwise. Then apply the exhortation to the hearers, that whoever is unfeeling and unkind has no proper knowledge of a God whose name is mercy.

Do not be troubled that the letter referred to has not survived. It cannot be supposed that everything written to particular persons or churches was preserved, and the first epistle plainly is not meant, since it says nothing about relieving the ministers who came from Judea. Report the variants -- one copy reads that he wrote something to the church, the Latin that he would have written, the Syriac that he desired to write -- and leave the reader to weigh them. Then press the exhortation where it lands hardest. What is not to be imitated is the pride, the ambition, the love of preeminence and the hardheartedness just described; and note how far the example of men in office carries, especially in matters of charity, where following it lets a man keep his money and feel excused.

The uncomfortable point is who this man was, so make it: here is an officer of the church less generous, catholic and communicative than the private Christians in it, and ministers may sometimes be outshone and outdone. Say plainly that it is an ill and unbeseeming character in Christ's ministers to love preeminence and affect presidency in the church of God, and that this ferment sprang and wrought early. Trace the sequence -- ambition breeds malice against those who oppose it, and malice in the heart vents itself by the lips, so that the heart and the mouth are both to be watched. Observe that to an aspiring spirit apostolical authority signifies little. And state the limit that the whole episode exists to establish: the pastor is not at absolute liberty, nor lord over God's heritage.

debates.question: Did the apostle write to the church, or only wish to?

sides.position: He would have written, some manuscripts supplying the particle and judicious critics thinking it implied; he knew his letter must pass through hands that would not acknowledge his authority, and wrote to Gaius instead
He wrote. The reading requiring the other rendering is not sustained by good authority, and the plain sense of the verb without the particle is that he wrote
A few manuscripts add the particle; it is clearly spurious
The Latin reads that he would have written and the Syriac that he desired to write, while one copy reads that he wrote something to the church
His ambition does not prove him a bishop set over elders, as was true in the second century; he may have been an elder or a deacon, but clearly desired to rule the whole church
Doubtless an officer, at least a deacon and probably a bishop, who magnified himself in his office
Perhaps the pastor of the church
An officer and a minister, less generous, catholic and communicative than the private Christians of the same church

outliers.note: Alone reduces the conduct to the principle of the dog in the manger -- he would neither do nor let do, and when good was done that he did not approve he endeavoured to undo it -- and alone guesses at a motive, that the man may have been a converted Jew unwilling to see Gentiles received, or a Judaizing Christian who calumniated the apostles for teaching otherwise.

Alone makes the episode a lesson about ministers rather than about one man, observing that here is an officer less generous than the private Christians of his own church and that ministers may sometimes be outshone and outdone, tracing the sequence by which ambition breeds malice and malice vents itself by the lips, and stating the limit the whole affair exists to establish, that the pastor is not at absolute liberty nor lord over God's heritage.

Alone weighs what the verbs for hindering and casting out can bear, allowing that each may describe a single success, a repeated practice, or an attempt that failed; and alone remarks that the aged writer is not afraid of the man and openly defies him, and is the apostle of love for all that.

Alone explains why the letter referred to has not survived, holding that it cannot be supposed everything written to particular persons or churches was preserved, and alone rules out the first epistle on internal grounds, that it says nothing of relieving the ministers who came from Judea.

themes: I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not
Neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church
Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good

12.pericope_label: Demetrius hath good report of all men; greet the friends by name

schools.summary: Be candid that nothing is known of the man commended, and say what the alternatives cost: identifying him with the deserter of the Pauline letters is unlikely, and the identification with the Ephesian silversmith is one we should like to believe without evidence for it. He may have carried this letter and may have come under suspicion, which would account for so warm a commendation. Count the witnesses, three of them -- all men, the truth, and the writer with those about him -- and raise the possibility that the second is the Holy Spirit rather than a personification, since the Spirit is elsewhere called the truth. On the closing courtesies, note that the ordinary Greek farewell said be strong, that the word here was the greeting of the resurrection day, and that the instruction to greet each by name echoes the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name, the phrase occurring nowhere else in the New Testament though common in the papyrus letters.

Make the commendation itself the lesson. A name in the gospel and a fame in the churches is better than that of sons and daughters, and this man's character was his commendation. Take the three degrees of it in order: general, that he had a good report of all men; deserved, that the report was of the truth itself, for some have a good report but not of the truth; and confirmed, by the apostle's own testimony with an appeal to what the reader already knew. Add the two cautions -- that few are well spoken of by all and that it is sometimes ill to be so, and that it is well when those who commend a man can appeal to the consciences of those who know him best. Close on the ending, that many things are fitter for speech than for a letter, and that those may well greet one another on earth who hope to live together in heaven.

The material here is small-scale and precise, so use it that way. Set the writing materials of this letter against those of the last, ink and pen here where the other named paper and ink. Report the manuscript question at the close, that the older copies read brethren where the received text reads friends, the latter being a singular appellation found nowhere else in Scripture; and note that the word for friend seldom appears in the New Testament at all, being swallowed up in the more endearing name of brother. Then draw the inference the ending permits about the whole letter: a farewell that assumes personal acquaintance with a whole circle, to be greeted one by one, is not what a man writes to a city he has never visited.

sides.position: Possibly the same as Demas, of which this is the fuller name, or the man sent from Ephesus with this letter, or a member of the same church as Gaius

Nothing else is known; identification with Demas is unlikely, and with the Ephesian silversmith is something one would like to believe without evidence. He may be the bearer of the letter and may have come under suspicion
Probably a member of the same church as Gaius, since the phrase implies a testimony wider than the writer's own knowledge
Perhaps another member of that church, or one of those recommended, or the bearer of the letter

debates.question: Should the last verse read "the friends" or "the brethren"?

sides.position: The older copies read brethren; friends is a very singular appellation, found nowhere else in Scripture
The word friend does not often occur in the New Testament, being swallowed up in the more endearing name of brother
The appellation, uncommon in the New Testament, recalls the Lord's words in the upper room to those he would no longer call servants
The friends are those at Ephesus, known to the writer by name as the good shepherd calls his sheep

outliers.note: Alone observes that the closing wish was chosen against the ordinary Greek farewell, which said be strong, and that this word was the greeting of the resurrection day; he unfolds it in three, the inward peace of a good conscience, the outward peace of universal friendship, and the heavenly peace of future glory begun in this life.

Alone sets the writing materials of this letter against those of the last, ink and pen here where the other named paper and ink, and alone argues from the closing greetings that the letter cannot have been sent to Corinth, since it assumes a personal acquaintance with a whole circle to be greeted one by one and the writer is unlikely ever to have been in that city.

Alone counts the three witnesses to Demetrius as three -- all men, the truth, and the writer with those about him -- and raises the possibility that the second means the Holy Spirit rather than a personification of truth, since the Spirit is elsewhere called the truth.

Alone grades the commendation into three -- general, deserved, and confirmed by testimony appealing to what the reader already knew -- and alone states the caution that some have a good report but not of the truth itself, and that it is well when those who commend a man can appeal to the consciences of those who know him best.

themes: Demetrius hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself
I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee
Peace be to thee. Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name
